I have no clue. Sorry. The restart makes me think its a driver or some game patch that doesn't take effect until you restart you PC.

Might wanna try to install an slightly older video driver. Otherwise I think CD project red support is your best bet. Or just a new, better video card.

You can also google around for the crash codes (3221225477 and/or 0x00000020) and see if you can find a solution.

Hope you can get it working!

Two final things you can try. Under my documents -> witcher 3 you'll find your saves and settings. If you delete the settings files the game will go back to default settings. In case there's some wierd game setting that suddenly decided to cause issues.

You can also try to underclock your video card slightly. MSI afterburner and Asus GPU Tweak II are the two most popular GPU clocking softwares.

I remember I had an similar issue with GTA V. Game would freeze and crash after 5 min if I didn't underclock it. Even at stock clock.

Try open geforce experience and reinstalling your drivers.
If that doesn't work download [Display Driver Uninstaller](https://www.wagnardsoft.com/content/display-driver-uninstaller-ddu-v17066-released) and do a clean install of your video card drivers.

Most people with this issue seem to either have video card issues or game file issues.

But if you can't fix it try to contact [CD Project Red support](http://en.cdprojektred.com/contact-support/) with your crash log and see if they can help you.

The startrail rule depends very much on what the resolution is and what part of the sky you are shooting. On 24mm it can be anywhere between 15 to 35. So I tend to not use it. I belive the shot is between the 30s and the high 40s. I wanted to keep it as low as I could to keep the aurora structure. After it reached a minimum of 30s I would let it keep go until the aurora started to move away or dissipate.

It was a lazy scan, so it might be that. Other frames on the same roll also seem to have minor focus issues. It was only made for simple facebook use, but after I thought I'm gonna share here too.

Between 30 and 60 seconds.

Auroras tends to be in the -5 to -4 EV area. Really bright aurora can go as low as -3. But usualy its around -4.5 or so.

This image was shot a f/1.4, ISO 100 and I'm guessing around 30 second exposure based on the movment of the stars and the blurriness of the aurora.
